skills.objective: Students add, subtract, multiply and divide multidigit whole numbers using place value, and use estimates, the inverse operation and remainders to check that results make sense.
skills.studentObjective: I can work with big numbers by thinking about what each digit is worth, and I can check that my answer makes sense.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I solved a big-number problem using because, but and so with the words regroup, estimate and remainder.
successCriteria: I regroup correctly when I add or subtract across several places.
I multiply with partial products and keep each part in the right place.
I divide and say what the remainder means in the situation.
I use an estimate to explain why my answer is reasonable.
skills.bigIdea: Every digit has a place value, so big-number calculations are built from smaller, place-by-place pieces that can be checked.

syntax: I regrouped ___ because ___.
The remainder is ___, which means ___ are left over.
discourse: Describe each step of a calculation in order
Justify why an answer is reasonable

domains.listening: Students listen to a ticket count and tell where the speaker regroups and what the answer means.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner each step of a calculation and say how an estimate checks the answer.
domains.reading: Students read a food drive passage and underline each number and what it counts.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about a calculation with regrouping.

vocab.def: To trade 10 of one place-value unit for 1 of the next larger unit, or the reverse.
vocab.nonExample: Moving a digit to another column without trading
vocab.sentence: Mira has to regroup 15 ones as 1 ten and 5 ones.
vocab.morphology: re- means again; group means a set of things

vocab.def: The amount left over when a number cannot be shared into equal groups exactly.
vocab.sentence: The remainder is 5 cans, so those cans do not fill a box.

vocab.def: The answer to a multiplication problem.
vocab.nonExample: A jar of honey on a store shelf
vocab.sentence: The product of 6 and 1,055 is 6,330.
vocab.everyday: Something that is made or grown to be sold, like honey or tomatoes

vocab.def: To find a number close to the exact answer, often by rounding first.
vocab.sentence: Kofi can estimate before he adds.

vocab.def: The smaller products from multiplying one place-value part at a time, which you then add.
vocab.sentence: Add the partial products 200, 80, 30 and 12 to get 322.

misconceptions.belief: In subtraction, take the smaller digit from the larger digit in each place.
misconceptions.why: Students want every column to work without trading, and they forget that the top number is the one you start with.
misconceptions.fix: Build the top number with place-value blocks and take the bottom number away, trading a ten or a hundred when there are not enough pieces.

errorCase.story: Tavi subtracts 2,478 from 5,203.
steps: Line up 5,203 above 2,478.
In each place I take the smaller digit from the larger digit: 8 − 3 = 5, 7 − 0 = 7, 4 − 2 = 2 and 5 − 2 = 3.
errorCase.explain: Subtraction starts from the top number in every place. Regroup when the top digit is too small: 5,203 − 2,478 = 2,725.

misconceptions.belief: When you multiply by the tens digit, you can treat it as a single one.
misconceptions.why: Students multiply digit by digit and lose track of what each digit is worth.
misconceptions.fix: Write the digit as its value, 10 instead of 1, and use an area model so the 200, 80, 30 and 12 sit in their own parts.

errorCase.story: Zuri multiplies 23 × 14.
steps: Multiply 23 by the 4 in the ones place: 23 × 4 = 92.
Multiply 23 by the 1 in the tens place: 23 × 1 = 23.
Add the partial products: 92 + 23 = 115.
errorCase.explain: The 1 in 14 means 1 ten, so the partial product is 23 × 10 = 230. Then 92 + 230 = 322.

misconceptions.belief: If the divisor does not go into a digit, you can skip that place in the quotient.
misconceptions.why: Students think a zero is not a real digit, so they leave it out and the other digits slide into the wrong places.
misconceptions.fix: Estimate the size of the quotient first, then record a zero as a placeholder so every digit stays in its own place.

errorCase.story: Idris divides 4,236 by 4.
steps: 4 goes into 4 one time, so I write 1 in the thousands place.
4 does not go into 2, so I skip that place and use 23 instead: 23 ÷ 4 = 5 with 3 left.
I bring down the 6: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. The quotient is 159.
errorCase.explain: When 4 does not go into 2 hundreds, write 0 in the hundreds place. The quotient is 1,059, and 4 × 1,059 = 4,236.

misconceptions.belief: The answer to a division word problem is always the number after the R.
misconceptions.why: Students stop at the last number they wrote and do not reread the question to see what it asks.
misconceptions.fix: Say the question in your own words, then label every number in the division as boxes, cans or cans left over before you answer.

reading.title: The Food Drive
reading.text: Room 12 ran a food drive for the neighborhood pantry. In week one, students collected 3,476 cans. In week two, they collected 2,859 cans. Before adding, Kofi made an estimate: about 3,500 plus about 2,900 is about 6,400. Then he lined up the places and added. He had to regroup in the ones, the tens and the hundreds. The total was 6,335 cans, close to his estimate. Volunteers packed 6 cans in each box. Mira divided 6,335 by 6 and got 1,055 with a remainder of 5. She checked by multiplying. The product of 6 and 1,055 is 6,330, and 6,330 plus 5 is 6,335. So the pantry received 1,055 full boxes, and 5 cans stayed on the table.
reading.simple: Room 12 ran a food drive. In week one, students collected 3,476 cans. In week two, they collected 2,859 cans. Kofi made an estimate first: about 3,500 plus about 2,900 is about 6,400. Then he added and had to regroup. The total was 6,335 cans. Volunteers put 6 cans in each box. Mira divided 6,335 by 6 and got 1,055 with a remainder of 5. She checked: the product of 6 and 1,055 is 6,330. Then 6,330 plus 5 is 6,335. There were 1,055 full boxes and 5 cans left.

questions.q: How many cans did students collect in week two?
questions.a: 2,859 cans

questions.q: Why does Mira add 5 to 6,330 when she checks her division?
questions.a: The 5 is the remainder, the cans left over, so the cans in full boxes plus the leftover cans must equal 6,335.

questions.q: Why is 6,335 a reasonable total?
questions.a: It is close to Kofi's estimate of about 6,400, so the answer makes sense.

wdntb.why: The first three use the same fact family of 3,476, 2,859 and 6,335 with addition or subtraction. 6,335 ÷ 6 is the only one that divides and has a remainder.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at 3,476 + 2,859 with small 1s written above the tens, hundreds and thousands places. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: When you divide a whole number by 6, the remainder is smaller than 6.
asn.why: A remainder of 6 or more would make one more group of 6, so the remainder can only be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5.

asn.claim: The product of two whole numbers is greater than both numbers.
asn.why: 6 × 4 = 24 is greater than both, but 6 × 1 = 6 is not greater than 6, and 6 × 0 = 0 is smaller than 6.

wyr.q: Would you rather add 3,476 and 2,859 with the standard algorithm or by adding thousands, hundreds, tens and ones separately?

compare.a: Ana multiplies 23 × 14 with an area model: 200, 80, 30 and 12, then adds to get 322.
compare.b: Ben stacks the numbers: 23 × 4 = 92 and 23 × 10 = 230, then adds to get 322.
compare.prompt: Both strategies give the same product. How are they alike, and where does each one show the tens?

debate.claim: Estimating first is worth the time.
debate.forEvidence: Kofi's estimate of about 6,400 showed him that a total like 5,225 was too small and needed another look.
debate.againstEvidence: Estimating takes extra time, and the standard algorithm already gives the exact answer.

listening.script: Listen to Omar count tickets for the town fair. We printed 4,200 tickets, and we sold 1,375 of them. To find how many are left, I subtract 1,375 from 4,200. There are zeros in the tens and the ones, so I regroup from the hundreds. Now I can subtract in every place, and I get 2,825 tickets left. To check, I add: 2,825 plus 1,375 is 4,200. My friend Lila says the answer is 3,175. She took the smaller digit from the larger digit in each place. That cannot work, because we always start from the top number.

tasks.q: How many tickets are left?
tasks.why: Omar regroups and subtracts to get 2,825, and he checks that 2,825 plus 1,375 is 4,200.

tasks.q: Lila says 3,175. What went wrong?
options: She took the smaller digit from the larger digit in each place instead of regrouping.
She added the two numbers instead of subtracting.
tasks.why: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger digit ignores which number you start with, so the result is wrong.

story.title: The Pantry Count
story.goal: report the right number of cans and boxes to the pantry truck driver
story.intro: Kofi's class has two huge piles of canned food in the school lobby. The pantry truck arrives at noon, and Kofi must tell the driver the total and how many boxes are full.

beats.lead: Kofi combines the cans from week one and week two and thinks about what a sensible total would look like.
beats.success: The total is close to his estimate, so Kofi writes it on the delivery form.
beats.redirect: The total is far from his estimate, so Kofi lines up the places again and looks for a missed regroup.

beats.lead: Mira starts packing the cans into boxes and Kofi checks her work with the inverse operation.
beats.success: The check matches the total exactly, so Mira closes the boxes with a smile.
beats.redirect: The check is off by a few cans, so Mira rereads each place of the quotient and fixes a missing zero.

beats.lead: The driver asks what the leftover cans mean for the delivery.
beats.success: Kofi explains that the remainder is cans, not boxes, and the driver nods.
beats.redirect: Kofi pauses, rereads the question and decides again whether the number is boxes or cans.

story.ending: The truck leaves full, and Kofi can explain every number on the delivery form.

panels.says: I added 3,476 and 2,859 and got 5,225.
Let us estimate first. About 3,500 plus about 2,900 is about 6,400.
My answer is far from 6,400. I must have forgotten to regroup.
Yes! 6 + 9 is 15, so write 5 and trade 10 ones for 1 ten.
Now I get 6,335, which is close to my estimate.

predict.q: Kofi's total is 5,225. Before Mira answers, predict what an estimate will tell him.
options: The total should be about 6,400, so 5,225 is too small.
The total should be about 5,200, so 5,225 is correct.
An estimate cannot tell him anything about the total.
predict.why: 3,476 is close to 3,500 and 2,859 is close to 2,900, so the total is close to 6,400.

transfer.relationship: Total = number of full groups × group size + what is left over
phrasings: 6,335 cans packed 6 to a box make 1,055 boxes with 5 cans left over
1,055 groups of 6 use 6,330 cans, and 5 cans are not enough for another group

decoys.text: 6,335 cans make 1,055 boxes with 5 boxes left over
decoys.why: The leftover 5 counts cans, not boxes, so the unit is wrong.
6 × 1,055 is 6,330, so this leaves out the 5 cans left over.

modeling.title: Planning the pantry delivery
modeling.scenario: A fictional school has collected 6,335 cans for a pantry. Volunteers pack 6 cans in each box, and a small truck can carry 900 boxes on each trip.
assumptions: Every full box holds exactly 6 cans.
Cans that do not fill a box stay at school this week.
The truck can only carry full boxes.
prompts: How many full boxes can the volunteers pack, and how many cans are left over?
How many trips does the truck need for all the full boxes?
What would change if each box held 5 cans instead of 6?
limits: Real cans differ in size, so not every box would hold exactly 6 cans.
We ignored the time it takes to pack and load the boxes.

sentence.because: The total is 6,335 because I had to regroup in the ones, the tens and the hundreds.
sentence.but: My estimate was about 6,400, but the exact total is 6,335.
sentence.so: I regrouped in three places, so the total is 6,335.

diagnostic.prompt: Solve 4,206 − 1,758 and 34 × 26. For each one, say how you know the answer is reasonable.
lookFor: Regroups across a zero when subtracting
Uses partial products with the correct place value
Gives an estimate before or after calculating
diagnostic.language: Let the student show each step with place-value blocks or a drawing before explaining aloud. If the steps are right, the barrier is describing them, not calculating.

extension.task: Write a food drive problem that ends with a remainder, solve it, and write one question whose answer is the quotient and another whose answer is the remainder.
extension.reasoning: Explain why a division by 7 can never have a remainder of 7.

en.learning: Your child is learning to add, subtract, multiply and divide big numbers by understanding what each digit is worth.
en.say: Make an estimate first, then check whether the exact answer is close to it.
en.ask: If we have 200 pencils and put 6 in each bag, how many full bags can we make and how many pencils are left over?
en.activity: Count two jars of beans together. Estimate the total, add the two counts, and compare the answer with your estimate.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a sumar, restar, multiplicar y dividir números grandes entendiendo cuánto vale cada dígito.
es.say: Primero hagan una estimación y después revisen si la respuesta exacta se acerca a ella.
es.ask: Si tenemos 200 lápices y ponemos 6 en cada bolsa, ¿cuántas bolsas llenas podemos armar y cuántos lápices sobran?
es.activity: Cuenten juntos los frijoles de dos frascos. Estimen el total, sumen los dos conteos y comparen el resultado con la estimación.

skills.objective: Students interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, tell the difference between comparing with equal groups and comparing by how much more, and solve comparison problems with an unknown using drawings and equations.
skills.studentObjective: I can say how many times as many one amount is than another and tell that apart from how many more.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain a comparison using because, but and so with the words times as many, more than and equation.
successCriteria: I read an equation like 24 = 4 × 6 as a comparison sentence.
I tell a multiplicative comparison from an additive comparison.
I draw a tape diagram that matches the comparison.
I find the unknown amount and say what the answer means.
skills.bigIdea: Comparing with times as many asks how many equal groups of the smaller amount make the larger amount, while comparing with more than asks how much extra there is.

syntax: ___ is ___ times as many as ___.
___ is ___ more than ___, but ___ is ___ times as many as ___.
discourse: Contrast two kinds of comparison
Justify which amount is the larger one

domains.listening: Students listen to a ribbon story and decide which ribbon was found by multiplying and which by adding.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner which amount is the smaller one and how many equal groups they need.
domains.reading: Students read a shelter report and mark each comparison as equal groups or extra.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares two amounts.

vocab.def: A way to compare where the larger amount is made of equal groups of the smaller amount.
vocab.example: 24 cats is 4 times as many as 6 dogs
vocab.nonExample: 24 cats is 18 more than 6 dogs, which tells how much extra
vocab.sentence: There are 4 times as many cats as dogs.

vocab.def: A way to compare that tells how much extra one amount has over another.
vocab.nonExample: 12 rabbits is 2 times as many as 6 dogs, which uses equal groups
vocab.sentence: There are 6 more rabbits than dogs.

vocab.def: In multiplication, a word that tells how many equal groups there are.
vocab.nonExample: The bus comes at two different times
vocab.sentence: Pilar says that 4 times 6 is 24.
vocab.everyday: A moment on the clock, or how often something happens, like three times a day

vocab.def: A number sentence with an equals sign that says two amounts are the same.
vocab.sentence: The equation 24 = 4 × 6 compares 24 to 6.

vocab.def: A number you do not know yet, often written as a letter or a box.
vocab.example: In 24 = n × 6, the unknown is n
vocab.nonExample: The 6 in 24 = n × 6, which is given
vocab.sentence: Pilar finds the unknown number of times.
vocab.morphology: un- means not; known means understood

misconceptions.belief: '3 times as many' means add 3 to the smaller amount.
misconceptions.why: Students know 'more' from adding and hear 'times as many' as another kind of more.
misconceptions.fix: Draw the smaller amount as one tape and repeat it, then compare 3 equal tapes with one tape and a small extra piece.

errorCase.story: A shelter has 4 rabbits and 3 times as many cats as rabbits.
steps: Rabbits are 4, and cats are 3 times as many.
Times as many means add, so 4 + 3 = 7.
There are 7 cats.
errorCase.explain: 3 times as many means 3 equal groups of 4, so 3 × 4 = 12 cats. Seven would only be 3 more than 4.

misconceptions.belief: When the larger amount is given, multiply it by the number of times to find the smaller amount.
misconceptions.why: Students see a number and 'times' and multiply without asking which amount is the larger one.
misconceptions.fix: Label the tapes first: the larger amount is the whole row of equal parts, so find one part by dividing.

errorCase.story: A red ribbon is 5 times as long as a blue ribbon, and the red ribbon is 40 cm long.
steps: Red is 5 times as long as blue, and red is 40 cm.
Multiply: 5 × 40 = 200.
The blue ribbon is 200 cm.
errorCase.explain: The red ribbon is the larger amount, made of 5 equal blue lengths. Divide 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so the blue ribbon is 8 cm.

misconceptions.belief: To say how many times as many, subtract the two numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students use subtraction for every comparison because it answers 'how much more'.
misconceptions.fix: Ask how many groups of the smaller number fit in the larger number, and count the groups on a tape diagram.

errorCase.story: Rosa compares 24 and 6.
steps: I want to compare 24 and 6.
So 24 is 18 times as many as 6.
errorCase.explain: The 18 tells how much more 24 is than 6. To find how many times as many, ask how many 6s make 24: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

misconceptions.belief: An equation like 24 = 4 × 6 is written backwards because the answer should come last.
misconceptions.why: Students read equations left to right and expect the answer to come right after the equals sign.
misconceptions.fix: Read the equation as a sentence, 24 is 4 times as many as 6, and match each part to a tape diagram.

reading.title: Counting at the Shelter
reading.text: At the Maple Street Animal Shelter, volunteer Pilar counts the animals. There are 6 dogs. There are 4 times as many cats as dogs, so she writes the equation 4 × 6 = 24. There are 6 more rabbits than dogs, so she writes 6 + 6 = 12. Her cousin Tomás thinks both sentences use the same idea. Pilar draws a tape diagram. For the cats, she draws 4 equal tapes, and each one is as long as the dog tape. For the rabbits, she draws one dog tape and a short extra piece of 6. The pictures look different because the comparisons are different. Then she writes 24 = n × 6 to find the unknown number of times, and n is 4.
reading.simple: At an animal shelter, Pilar counts the animals. There are 6 dogs. There are 4 times as many cats as dogs, so she writes the equation 4 × 6 = 24. There are 6 more rabbits than dogs, so she writes 6 + 6 = 12. In her tape diagram, the cats are 4 equal tapes, each as long as the dog tape. The rabbits are one dog tape and an extra piece of 6. Then she finds the unknown number of times: 24 = n × 6, and n is 4.

questions.q: How many cats are at the shelter?
questions.a: 24 cats

questions.q: Why do the tape diagrams for the cats and the rabbits look different?
questions.a: The cats are 4 equal tapes the size of the dog tape, but the rabbits are one dog tape plus an extra piece of 6.

questions.q: In 24 = n × 6, what does n tell you, and what is its value?
questions.a: n is how many times as many cats there are as dogs, and n is 4 because 4 × 6 = 24.

wdntb.why: 6 + 6 = 12 is the only one that compares by adding extra. The other three all describe how 24 and 6 are related by equal groups.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two tape diagrams for 6 dogs: 4 equal tapes of 6 for the cats, and one tape of 6 plus a piece of 6 for the rabbits. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If A is 3 times as many as B and B is more than 0, then A is greater than B.
asn.why: A is made of 3 equal groups of B, so A is bigger than a single group of B.

asn.claim: If A and B are whole numbers and A is 5 more than B, then A is also 5 times as many as B.
asn.why: Try numbers: 5 more than 4 is 9 but 5 times 4 is 20, and 5 more than 1 is 6 but 5 times 1 is 5. The two never match.

wyr.q: Would you rather show '4 times as many cats as dogs' with a tape diagram or with an equation?

compare.a: Nia says 24 is 18 more than 6 because 24 − 6 = 18.
compare.b: Omar says 24 is 4 times as many as 6 because 6 × 4 = 24.
compare.prompt: Are both sentences true? What does each one tell you about 24 and 6?

debate.claim: 'More than' and 'times as many' tell you the same thing about two numbers.
debate.forEvidence: Both phrases compare two amounts, and both say that the first amount is the larger one.
debate.againstEvidence: 6 more than 6 is 12, but 6 times as many as 6 is 36, so the two phrases give different amounts.

listening.script: Listen to Keiko talk about ribbons for a craft fair. My blue ribbon is 9 inches long. My green ribbon is 4 times as long as the blue ribbon, so I think of 4 groups of 9 inches. Four times nine is 36, so the green ribbon is 36 inches long. My friend Sam has a red ribbon that is 12 inches longer than the blue one, so his ribbon is 21 inches long. Both of our ribbons are longer than the blue ribbon, but we found the lengths in different ways. I used equal groups, and Sam added the extra part.

tasks.q: How long is the green ribbon?
tasks.why: The green ribbon is 4 groups of 9 inches, and 4 × 9 = 36.

tasks.q: Which sentence correctly describes the red ribbon?
options: The red ribbon is 12 inches longer than the blue ribbon.
The red ribbon is 12 times as long as the blue ribbon.
The red ribbon is 4 times as long as the blue ribbon.
tasks.why: Sam added 12 inches to the blue ribbon, so the red ribbon is longer by 12 inches. It is not made of equal groups.

story.title: The Shelter Count
story.goal: write a weekly report that compares each kind of animal with the dogs
story.intro: Pilar helps at the animal shelter every Saturday. The director wants a short report that compares the number of cats, rabbits and birds with the number of dogs.

beats.lead: Pilar draws a tape diagram for the cats and works out how many dog-sized tapes she needs.
beats.success: The tape diagram matches the sentence, so Pilar writes the right equation in the report.
beats.redirect: The diagram shows too few equal tapes, so Pilar rereads the sentence and counts the groups again.

beats.lead: Tomás reads the note about the rabbits and wonders whether to multiply or add.
beats.success: He sees that the note says how much more, so he adds and the report agrees.
beats.redirect: His answer looks too big, so he checks whether the note talks about equal groups or about extra.

beats.lead: The director asks Pilar to explain how she knows which comparison is which.
beats.success: Pilar points to her tapes and explains the difference in one clear sentence.
beats.redirect: Pilar pauses, reads each comparison sentence aloud and matches it to a picture.

story.ending: The shelter board approves the report, and Pilar can tell any visitor how two amounts compare.

panels.says: There are 6 dogs, and there are 4 times as many cats.
So there are 4 more cats than dogs, which is 6 + 4 = 10.
Let us draw it. Times as many means equal groups of 6, not an extra 4.
Oh! Four groups of 6 make 24 cats.
Yes, and the equation 24 = 4 × 6 says the same thing.

predict.q: Pilar says there are 4 times as many cats as the 6 dogs. Predict how many cats there are.
predict.why: Four equal groups of 6 make 4 × 6 = 24 cats.

transfer.relationship: The larger amount is a number of equal groups of the smaller amount
phrasings: There are 4 times as many cats as dogs
24 = 4 × 6, with 24 cats and 6 dogs
A tape of 6 dogs repeated 4 times makes 24 cats
24 ÷ 6 = 4, so the cats are 4 times the number of dogs

decoys.text: There are 18 more cats than dogs
decoys.why: This is true, but it tells how much extra, not how many equal groups.

decoys.text: There are 4 times as many dogs as cats
decoys.why: The comparison is reversed, because the dogs are the smaller amount.

modeling.title: Planning shelter supplies
modeling.scenario: A fictional animal shelter has 6 dogs and expects 4 times as many cats as dogs next month. Each cat eats 3 scoops of food a day.
assumptions: Every cat eats the same amount each day.
The number of dogs stays at 6.
No cat leaves or arrives during the month.
prompts: How many cats will the shelter have?
How many scoops of cat food does the shelter need each day?
What would change if the shelter had 5 times as many cats as dogs?
limits: Real animals are adopted and arrive all the time, so the counts would change.
Some cats may eat more or less than 3 scoops, so the food total is only a plan.

sentence.base: The cats are 4 times as many as the dogs.
sentence.because: The cats are 4 times as many as the dogs because 4 groups of 6 make 24 and there are 6 dogs.
sentence.but: There are 6 more rabbits than dogs, but there are 4 times as many cats as dogs.
sentence.so: There are 4 equal groups of 6 cats, so the cats are 4 times as many as the dogs.

diagnostic.prompt: A red ribbon is 7 cm long. A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. A green ribbon is 3 cm longer than the red ribbon. Draw both comparisons and tell how long each ribbon is.
lookFor: Draws 3 equal parts for the blue ribbon but one part plus a small piece for the green ribbon
Writes 3 × 7 = 21 for the blue ribbon and 7 + 3 = 10 for the green ribbon
Says in a sentence how 'times as long' and 'longer than' differ
diagnostic.language: Ask the student to point to the parts of the tape diagram while speaking. A correct drawing with a hesitant explanation suggests a language barrier with 'times as long', not a gap in the mathematics.

extension.task: Make up two comparisons about a group of 8 animals: one that uses 5 times as many and one that uses 5 more than. Find both amounts and draw a tape diagram for each.
extension.reasoning: Explain why 5 times as many as 8 is 40 but 5 more than 8 is only 13.

en.learning: Your child is learning to compare two numbers by asking how many equal groups there are, not only how many more.
en.say: Three times as many means three equal groups of the smaller amount.
en.ask: I have 5 stickers and you have 4 times as many. How many stickers do you have, and how do you know?
en.activity: Line up pairs of socks or spoons. Make one pile that is 3 times as big as another, then a pile that is 3 more. Talk about how the piles look different.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a comparar dos números preguntando cuántos grupos iguales hay, no solo cuántos más.
es.say: Decir tres veces la cantidad quiere decir tres grupos iguales de la cantidad más pequeña.
es.ask: Yo tengo 5 calcomanías y tú tienes 4 veces esa cantidad. ¿Cuántas calcomanías tienes y cómo lo sabes?
es.activity: Alineen pares de calcetines o de cucharas. Hagan un montón que tenga 3 veces la cantidad de otro, y luego un montón que tenga 3 más. Hablen de cómo se ven diferentes los montones.

skills.objective: Students find all factor pairs of a whole number from 1 to 100, recognize multiples, and decide whether a number is prime or composite by reasoning about its factors.
skills.studentObjective: I can find every factor of a number, tell what its multiples are, and say whether it is prime or composite.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I know a number is prime or composite using because, but and so with the words factor, multiple and prime number.
successCriteria: I list every factor pair of a number up to 100 in an organized way.
I name multiples of a number by counting by that number.
I use factors to decide if a number is prime or composite.
I use the words factor and multiple correctly in a sentence.
skills.bigIdea: A number can be built from equal groups in as many ways as it has factor pairs, and the factors tell us whether the number is prime or composite.

syntax: ___ is a factor of ___ because ___ × ___ = ___.
___ is a multiple of ___ because ___ groups of ___ make ___.
discourse: Explain a systematic search for factors
Classify a number and justify the choice

domains.listening: Students listen to a chair-setup story and tell which row counts leave chairs over.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they found every factor pair and how they know none is missing.
domains.reading: Students read a garden passage and circle each factor pair.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that classifies a number.

vocab.def: A whole number that multiplies with another whole number to make a given number.
vocab.sentence: Amara lists every factor of 24.
vocab.everyday: Something that helps cause a result, like weather being a factor in a game

vocab.def: A number you get when you multiply a given number by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
vocab.sentence: The number 24 is a multiple of 6.

vocab.def: Two whole numbers that multiply to make a given number.
vocab.sentence: The factor pair 4 and 6 makes an array with 4 rows and 6 columns.

vocab.def: A whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
vocab.sentence: A prime number can only be arranged in one array without turning it.

vocab.def: A whole number greater than 1 with more than two factors.
vocab.sentence: The composite number 24 can make many different arrays.
vocab.morphology: composite means made of several parts

misconceptions.belief: A factor pair gives only the smaller factor, so the larger factor can be left off the list.
misconceptions.why: Students stop listing once they pass the middle of the search and forget that each pair gives two factors, including the number itself.
misconceptions.fix: Write each pair as a multiplication fact and copy both numbers onto the list, then count the factors against the number of pairs.

errorCase.story: Noor lists the factors of 18.
steps: Factors come in pairs: 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6.
I tested 4, 5, 7 and 8, and none of them go into 18.
The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, so there are 5.
errorCase.explain: Each pair gives two factors, and 18 is a factor of itself. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18, so there are 6.

misconceptions.belief: The numbers that divide into 6 are the multiples of 6.
misconceptions.why: Factor and multiple are both new, similar-sounding words, and students swap which one goes up and which one goes down.
misconceptions.fix: Link each word to an action: factors are found by breaking a number into equal groups, multiples are found by counting by the number.

errorCase.story: Beto lists the first four multiples of 6.
steps: Multiples of 6 are connected to 6.
I think of numbers that go into 6: 1, 2, 3 and 6.
The first four multiples of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
errorCase.explain: Multiples come from counting by 6: 6, 12, 18 and 24. The numbers that go into 6 are its factors.

misconceptions.belief: Every odd number is prime.
misconceptions.why: Students notice that 3, 5, 7 and 11 are odd and prime and conclude that odd causes prime.
misconceptions.fix: Test odd numbers by looking for a factor pair other than 1 and the number, such as 3 × 3 for 9 and 3 × 5 for 15.

errorCase.story: Pia decides whether 9 is prime.
steps: The number 9 is odd.
Odd numbers are prime, so 9 is prime.
errorCase.explain: Odd numbers are not always prime. Since 3 × 3 = 9, the number 9 has three factors, 1, 3 and 9, so it is composite.

misconceptions.belief: The number 1 is prime because nothing else goes into it.
misconceptions.why: Students learn that a prime has few factors and think fewer is always better.
misconceptions.fix: List the factors of 1 and of 13 and count them: a prime needs exactly two, and 1 has only one.

reading.title: Rows in the Garden
reading.text: The garden club has 24 seedlings to plant in equal rows. Amara wants to find every way to make a rectangle. She starts with a factor pair: 1 and 24 make one long row. Then she tries 2 and 12, 3 and 8, and 4 and 6. Each pair multiplies to make 24, so 24 has eight factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. A second bed has 13 seedlings. Amara finds only one pair, 1 and 13. A prime number has exactly two factors, so 13 is prime. A number with more than two factors is a composite number, so 24 is composite. Amara also notices that 24 is a multiple of 6, because 4 groups of 6 make 24.
reading.simple: The garden club has 24 seedlings. Amara wants every way to plant them in equal rows. The factor pairs are 1 and 24, 2 and 12, 3 and 8, and 4 and 6. So 24 has the factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. A second bed has 13 seedlings. Only the pair 1 and 13 works, so 13 is a prime number. Since 24 has more than two factors, it is a composite number. Also, 24 is a multiple of 6, because 4 groups of 6 make 24.

questions.q: How many factors does 24 have?
questions.a: Eight factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24.

questions.q: Why is 13 a prime number but 24 a composite number?
questions.a: 13 has only two factors, 1 and 13, but 24 has more than two factors.

questions.q: How do you know 24 is a multiple of 6?
questions.a: Counting by 6 reaches 24, and 4 × 6 = 24.

wdntb.why: 13, 17 and 23 are prime numbers. 21 is composite because 3 × 7 = 21, so it has more than two factors.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the arrays for 24 seedlings: 1 by 24, 2 by 12, 3 by 8 and 4 by 6. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A whole number greater than 2 that is even is prime.
asn.why: An even number greater than 2 has the factor 2 as well as 1 and itself, so it has at least three factors.

asn.claim: A multiple of 4 is also a multiple of 8.
asn.why: 16 is a multiple of both 4 and 8, but 12 is a multiple of 4 and is not a multiple of 8.

wyr.q: Would you rather find factor pairs by building arrays or by writing multiplication facts?

compare.a: Dara tests 1, 2, 3 and so on in order to see which numbers go into 36, and stops at 6.
compare.b: Eli finds one pair, like 4 × 9, and uses it to write two factors at once.
compare.prompt: Both find the factors of 36. Why can Dara stop at 6, and why does Eli's way give two factors each time?

debate.claim: A class of 24 is easier to split into teams than a class of 23.
debate.forEvidence: 24 can be split into equal teams of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 or 12, but 23 can only be split into teams of 1 or 23.
debate.againstEvidence: A class of 23 can still make teams if one team is a little different, and many tasks do not need equal teams.

listening.script: Listen to Mr. Reyes set up chairs for the school play. He has 36 chairs and wants equal rows with none left over. He tries 4 rows, and that works with 9 chairs in each row, because 4 times 9 is 36. He tries 5 rows, but 5 times 7 is only 35, so one chair is left over. That means 5 is not a factor of 36. Then he tries 6 rows with 6 chairs in each row, because 6 times 6 is 36. Mr. Reyes says that 36 is a multiple of 4, a multiple of 6 and a multiple of 9.

tasks.q: Which number of rows leaves one chair left over?
tasks.why: 5 × 7 = 35, so 5 rows leave 1 chair of the 36 without a place.

tasks.q: Which row counts did Mr. Reyes find that work with no chairs left over?
tasks.why: 4 × 9 = 36 and 6 × 6 = 36 both work, but 5 does not go into 36 evenly.

story.title: Rows for the Spring Garden
story.goal: plant every seedling in equal rows with none left over
story.intro: The garden club has trays of seedlings to plant before the rain. Amara wants each bed to have equal rows, so she must decide how to arrange every tray.

beats.lead: Amara counts the first tray and starts listing the factor pairs of the number of seedlings.
beats.success: Her list has a partner for every factor, so she picks a row plan that fits the bed.
beats.redirect: One factor has no partner on her list, so Amara multiplies again to find the missing pair.

beats.lead: Diego brings a tray with 17 seedlings and asks whether it can make equal rows.
beats.success: Amara tests each small number and shows that only one long row works, so 17 is prime.
beats.redirect: Diego thinks every odd number is prime, so Amara tests another odd number to check.

beats.lead: The club president asks which bed sizes are multiples of 6.
beats.success: Amara counts by 6 and marks every bed size that lands on the list.
beats.redirect: Amara mixes up factors and multiples, so she rereads the question and counts by 6 instead.

story.ending: Every seedling has a place, and Amara can tell the club why each row plan works.

panels.says: I have 18 bean plants, and I can plant them in 2 rows of 9.
So 2 and 9 are the only factors of 18, because 2 × 9 = 18.
Not so fast. Let me list every pair: 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6.
Now I see six factors: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.
And 18 is a multiple of every one of them.

predict.q: Amara wants 18 bean plants in equal rows with none left over. Predict which number of rows works.
predict.why: 6 × 3 = 18, so 6 is a factor of 18. Four rows and five rows leave plants over.

transfer.relationship: A number is made of equal groups, so its factor pairs show every way to arrange it
phrasings: 24 seedlings can be planted in 4 rows of 6
4 × 6 = 24, so 4 and 6 are a factor pair of 24
24 is a multiple of 4 and a multiple of 6
24 ÷ 4 = 6 with nothing left over

decoys.why: A factor of a whole number is never greater than the number, so the words are reversed.

decoys.text: 24 seedlings can be planted in 5 rows of 5
decoys.why: 5 × 5 = 25, so five rows of five would need one more seedling.

modeling.title: Planning garden beds
modeling.scenario: A fictional garden club has 36 seedlings. It wants to plant them in equal rows with no seedlings left over, but the plot has room for at most 9 rows.

given.label: Most rows the plot can hold

assumptions: Every row has the same number of seedlings.
No seedling is left out or planted twice.
The rows are all as long as the longest one needs to be.
prompts: List every way to plant 36 seedlings in equal rows with none left over.
Which of those plans fit a plot with at most 9 rows?
What would change if the club found 1 more seedling and had 37?
limits: Real plants need space, so very long rows may not be possible.
We ignored the space between rows and the shape of the plot.

sentence.because: The number 13 is prime because its only factor pair is 1 and 13.
sentence.but: The number 24 is bigger than 13, but 24 is composite and 13 is prime.
sentence.so: The number 24 has more than two factors, so it is a composite number.

diagnostic.prompt: List every factor pair of 30 and of 31. Tell which number is prime and which is composite, and how you know.
lookFor: Finds the four factor pairs of 30: 1 and 30, 2 and 15, 3 and 10, 5 and 6
Says 31 has only the pair 1 and 31
Uses the words factor and multiple correctly
diagnostic.language: Let the student build each number with tiles in equal rows before explaining. If the arrays are correct but factor and multiple get swapped, the barrier is vocabulary.

extension.task: Find a number less than 50 that has exactly six factors, and show all of its factor pairs.
extension.reasoning: Explain why 36 has an odd number of factors but 24 has an even number of factors.

en.learning: Your child is learning about factors and multiples, and about prime and composite numbers.
en.say: A factor pair is two numbers that multiply to make another number, like 3 and 8 for 24.
en.ask: How many different ways can we put 12 crackers on plates so every plate has the same amount?
en.activity: Sort a handful of buttons or coins into equal rows. Find every way to do it with none left over, and write the multiplication fact for each way.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo sobre factores y múltiplos, y sobre números primos y compuestos.
es.say: Un par de factores son dos números que se multiplican para formar otro número, como 3 y 8 para formar 24.
es.ask: ¿De cuántas maneras podemos poner 12 galletas en platos para que cada plato tenga la misma cantidad?
es.activity: Acomoden un puñado de botones o monedas en filas iguales. Busquen todas las maneras sin que sobre ninguno y escriban la multiplicación de cada una.

skills.objective: Students generate equivalent fractions by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number, and compare fractions with different numerators and denominators using benchmarks or common denominators.
skills.studentObjective: I can write fractions that name the same amount and tell which of two fractions is greater.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why two fractions are equal or unequal using because, but and so with the words equivalent fractions, numerator and denominator.
successCriteria: I make an equivalent fraction by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number.
I show equal fractions with a strip or a number line.
I compare two fractions using a benchmark or a common denominator.
I write the comparison with greater than or less than and explain it in a sentence.
skills.bigIdea: Cutting the equal parts of a whole into smaller equal parts changes the names of the fraction but not its size, and fractions can be compared fairly only when the pieces are the same size.

syntax: ___ and ___ are equivalent fractions because both numbers were multiplied by ___.
___ is greater than ___ because ___.
discourse: Justify that two fractions name the same amount
Compare two quantities and defend the comparison

domains.listening: Students listen to a ribbon story and decide which fractions name the same amount.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they know which of two fractions is greater.
domains.reading: Students read a quilt passage and underline each fraction and the amount it names.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about equivalent fractions.

vocab.def: The top number of a fraction, which tells how many equal parts are counted.
vocab.sentence: The numerator tells how many parts are shaded.
vocab.morphology: from Latin numerare, meaning to count

vocab.def: The bottom number of a fraction, which tells how many equal parts make the whole.
vocab.sentence: The denominator of 6/8 is 8.

vocab.def: Fractions that name the same amount even though their numerators and denominators differ.
vocab.sentence: The fractions 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent fractions.
vocab.morphology: equi- means equal; valent means worth

vocab.def: A shared denominator that lets you compare fractions by looking only at their numerators.
vocab.example: 12 is a common denominator of 3/4 and 5/6
vocab.nonExample: The numbers 4 and 6, which are different denominators
vocab.sentence: Leila uses a common denominator to compare 3/4 and 5/6.

vocab.def: A familiar number, such as 1/2, used to judge how big another number is.
vocab.example: Using 1/2 to see that 3/8 is less than half
vocab.sentence: A benchmark like 1/2 helps you compare quickly.

vocab.def: A phrase that says one number is larger than another, written with the symbol >.
vocab.sentence: The fraction 10/12 is greater than 9/12.

misconceptions.belief: To make an equivalent fraction, add the same number to the numerator and the denominator.
misconceptions.why: Students know that adding the same amount keeps a difference, and they apply that idea to fractions.
misconceptions.fix: Fold a strip into halves, then into fourths, and see that each half is cut into pieces, which is multiplying, not adding.

errorCase.story: Mateo wants a fraction equivalent to 1/2.
steps: I want a fraction that equals 1/2.
I add 2 to the top and the bottom: 1 + 2 = 3 and 2 + 2 = 4.
So 3/4 is equivalent to 1/2.
errorCase.explain: Adding changes the size of the fraction. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number: 1 × 2 = 2 and 2 × 2 = 4, so 2/4 is equivalent to 1/2.

misconceptions.belief: A fraction with a bigger denominator is a bigger fraction.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the numerator and denominator as two whole numbers and think a bigger number means a bigger amount.
misconceptions.fix: Cut two same-sized strips into 3 parts and into 8 parts and compare one piece of each: more pieces means smaller pieces.

errorCase.story: Nina compares 1/3 of a ribbon with 1/8 of the same ribbon.
steps: Both fractions have 1 part.
8 is bigger than 3, so 1/8 is bigger than 1/3.
The bigger piece of ribbon is 1/8.
errorCase.explain: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more pieces, so each piece is smaller. One eighth is less than one third.

misconceptions.belief: If both the numerator and the denominator of one fraction are bigger, that fraction is bigger.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the tops and the bottoms separately, without thinking about the size of the pieces.
misconceptions.fix: Rename one fraction so both have the same denominator, then compare the numerators.

errorCase.story: Omar compares 3/4 and 5/8.
steps: 5 is greater than 3, and 8 is greater than 4.
Both numbers in 5/8 are bigger, so 5/8 is greater than 3/4.
errorCase.explain: Fractions with different denominators need pieces of the same size first. 3/4 = 6/8, and 5/8 is less than 6/8, so 3/4 is greater.

misconceptions.belief: The numerator is the bottom number and the denominator is the top number.
misconceptions.why: The two words look and sound alike, so students swap them and then read the fraction the wrong way.
misconceptions.fix: Link each word to a job: the denominator names the kind of piece, like fourths, and the numerator counts how many pieces.

reading.title: The Quilt Squares
reading.text: Leila and Marco are sewing quilt squares for the school craft fair. Leila finished 3/4 of her quilt. Marco finished 6/8 of his, and he thinks that is a different amount. Leila draws two fraction strips. She cuts each fourth into 2 equal pieces, so 3 fourths become 6 eighths. The numerator and the denominator both doubled, so 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent fractions. Rosa finished 5/6 of her quilt. To compare 5/6 with 3/4, Leila uses a common denominator of 12. She writes 3/4 as 9/12 and 5/6 as 10/12. Because 10/12 is greater than 9/12, Rosa has finished more of her quilt.
reading.simple: Leila and Marco sew quilt squares. Leila finished 3/4 of her quilt. Marco finished 6/8 of his. Leila cuts each fourth into 2 equal pieces, so 3 fourths become 6 eighths. The numerator and the denominator both doubled, so 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent fractions. Rosa finished 5/6 of her quilt. To compare 5/6 with 3/4, Leila uses a common denominator of 12. She writes 3/4 as 9/12 and 5/6 as 10/12. Since 10/12 is greater than 9/12, Rosa finished more.

questions.q: How much of her quilt did Rosa finish?
questions.a: 5/6 of her quilt

questions.q: Why did Leila cut each fourth into 2 equal pieces?
questions.a: She wanted pieces the same size as Marco's eighths, so she could see that 3/4 and 6/8 name the same amount.

questions.q: How does the common denominator 12 show that 5/6 is greater than 3/4?
questions.a: 5/6 = 10/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, and 10 twelfths is greater than 9 twelfths.

wdntb.why: 1/2, 2/4 and 3/6 are all equivalent fractions that name one half. 4/6 is equivalent to 2/3, so it names a different amount.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two fraction strips: one cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded, and one cut into 8 equal parts with 6 shaded. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If you multiply the numerator and denominator of a fraction by the same whole number greater than 1, the new fraction names the same amount.
asn.why: Each equal part is cut into more equal pieces, and you count the same share of the whole.

asn.claim: A fraction with a greater denominator is greater than a fraction with a smaller denominator.
asn.why: 7/8 is greater than 1/3, but 1/8 is less than 1/3. The numerators matter too.

wyr.q: Would you rather compare 2/5 and 5/8 with the benchmark 1/2 or with a common denominator of 40?

compare.a: Ivy makes 2/3 into 4/6 by multiplying the top and the bottom by 2.
compare.b: Sam makes 2/3 into 4/5 by adding 2 to the top and the bottom.
compare.prompt: Whose fraction is equivalent to 2/3? How can you show it with a fraction strip?

debate.claim: A common denominator is the only way to compare fractions.
debate.forEvidence: A common denominator works for every pair: 3/4 is 9/12 and 5/6 is 10/12, so you can compare the numerators.
debate.againstEvidence: A benchmark can be faster: 2/5 is less than 1/2 and 5/8 is greater than 1/2, so no common denominator is needed.

listening.script: Listen to Priya compare ribbons for a gift shop. I cut my ribbon into 3 equal parts and used 2 of them, so I used 2/3. My brother cut his ribbon into 6 equal parts and used 4 of them, so he used 4/6. We used the same amount, because each of my thirds is the same as 2 sixths. Now I compare with Kai, who used 3/8 of his ribbon. I know 3/8 is less than 1/2, because half of 8 is 4 and 3 is less than 4. I used more than half, so I used more ribbon than Kai.

tasks.q: Which fraction names the same amount as 2/3?
tasks.why: Each third is 2 sixths, so 2 thirds are 4 sixths.

tasks.q: Why is 3/8 less than 1/2?
options: Half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4.
Every fraction with an 8 in it is less than 1/2.
Eighths are always bigger than halves.
tasks.why: Four eighths make one half, so 3 eighths is less than one half.

story.title: The Quilt Corner
story.goal: sort the quilt blocks from least finished to most finished
story.intro: Leila's class is sewing one big quilt for the craft fair raffle. Every group finishes a different fraction of its block, and Leila must sort the groups by how much they have done.

beats.lead: Leila's group and Marco's group give her two fractions with different denominators and she needs to know if they match.
beats.success: She renames one fraction with equal-sized pieces and sees that the two amounts match.
beats.redirect: She is not sure, so she folds two paper strips into the same-sized pieces and checks again.

beats.lead: Rosa reports a third fraction, and Leila decides how to compare it with the first two.
beats.success: Leila picks a common denominator and Rosa's block lands in the right place in the line.
beats.redirect: Leila notices she compared only the numerators, so she renames the fractions and starts over.

beats.lead: The fair director asks Leila to explain her order of the blocks to the visitors.
beats.success: Leila explains each comparison in one clear sentence and the visitors cheer.
beats.redirect: Leila pauses, rereads her strips, and finds the words that explain which block is larger.

story.ending: The quilt blocks hang in order from least to most finished, and Leila can explain every comparison.

panels.says: I finished 6/8 of my quilt, so I have more than your 3/4.
Hmm. Let me cut each of my fourths into 2 equal pieces.
Now my quilt shows 6 eighths. The numerator and the denominator both doubled.
So 3/4 and 6/8 are the same amount. I was fooled by the bigger numbers!
That is why we compare pieces of the same size.

predict.q: Marco has finished 6/8 of his quilt and Leila has finished 3/4 of hers. Before Leila cuts the strip, predict who has finished more.
options: Marco, because 6 and 8 are bigger numbers.
Leila, because 4 is a smaller denominator.
predict.why: Both numbers in 3/4 were multiplied by 2 to make 6/8, so the two fractions name the same amount.

transfer.relationship: The same part of a whole can have different fraction names when the equal parts are cut smaller
phrasings: 3 out of 4 equal parts are shaded, and 6 out of 8 equal parts are shaded
3 fourths is the same amount as 6 eighths
On a number line, 3/4 and 6/8 land on the same point

decoys.why: The numerator and denominator are swapped, so 4/3 is greater than 1 and 3/4 is less than 1.
Both numbers got bigger, but 3/4 is 6/8, so 5/8 is a smaller amount.

modeling.title: Planning the quilt border
modeling.scenario: A fictional class is sewing a quilt border with 12 squares in a row. The fabric club has finished 3/4 of the row and the craft club has finished 5/6 of the same row.
assumptions: All the squares are the same size.
A square is either finished or not finished.
Both clubs work on the same row of 12 squares.
prompts: How many squares has each club finished?
Which club has finished more, and by how many squares?
What would change if the row had 24 squares?
limits: Real sewing is not exact, and a square might be half finished.
We ignored how long each square takes to sew.

sentence.because: The fractions 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent because both numbers in 3/4 were multiplied by 2.
sentence.but: The fractions 3/4 and 6/8 look different, but they name the same amount.
sentence.so: The common denominator of 3/4 and 5/6 is 12, so I can compare 9/12 and 10/12.

diagnostic.prompt: Write two fractions that are equivalent to 2/3. Then decide which is greater, 5/8 or 3/5, and explain how you know.
lookFor: Multiplies the numerator and the denominator by the same number
Uses a common denominator such as 40, or a benchmark, correctly
Writes the comparison with greater than or less than and explains it in a sentence
diagnostic.language: Let the student shade fraction strips before explaining. If the strips show equal-sized pieces correctly, the barrier is the words numerator, denominator and equivalent.

extension.task: Find a fraction that is between 1/2 and 3/4, and show how you know with a common denominator.
extension.reasoning: Explain why renaming both fractions with a larger common denominator lets you find even more fractions between them.

en.learning: Your child is learning that one amount can have different fraction names, like 1/2 and 4/8, and how to decide which of two fractions is greater.
en.say: Fractions can only be compared fairly when the pieces are the same size.
en.ask: Would you rather have 3/4 of a sandwich or 5/8 of the same sandwich? How can you tell?
en.activity: Fold two paper strips of the same length. Fold one into 4 parts and the other into 8 parts, and color 1/2 of each. Talk about how the equal amounts look.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que una misma cantidad puede tener distintos nombres de fracción, como 1/2 y 4/8, y a decidir cuál de dos fracciones es mayor.
es.say: Las fracciones se comparan bien solo cuando las partes tienen el mismo tamaño.
es.ask: ¿Qué prefieres: 3/4 de un sándwich o 5/8 del mismo sándwich? ¿Cómo lo sabes?
es.activity: Doblen dos tiras de papel del mismo largo. Doblen una en 4 partes y la otra en 8 partes, y coloreen 1/2 de cada una. Hablen de cómo se ven las cantidades iguales.

skills.objective: Students add and subtract fractions with like denominators, rename between mixed numbers and improper fractions, and multiply a fraction by a whole number by thinking of repeated unit fractions.
skills.studentObjective: I can add, subtract and multiply fractions by counting equal-sized pieces.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I added, subtracted or multiplied fractions using because, but and so with the words like denominators, improper fraction and mixed number.
successCriteria: I add and subtract fractions with like denominators and keep the denominator the same.
I decompose a fraction into a sum of unit fractions or a whole and a fraction.
I rename an improper fraction as a mixed number.
I multiply a whole number by a fraction and explain it as repeated groups.
skills.bigIdea: Fractions with the same denominator are made of equal-sized pieces, so we combine, remove or repeat the pieces by counting them while the size of the piece stays the same.

syntax: ___ eighths plus ___ eighths is ___ eighths.
___ is an improper fraction, and as a mixed number it is ___.
discourse: Describe how pieces are combined and why their size stays the same
Explain how two forms of the same amount match

domains.listening: Students listen to a punch recipe and tell how many sixths are in the pitcher and why the denominator stays 6.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how many pieces they counted and what size each piece was.
domains.reading: Students read a trail mix passage and underline each fraction and the ingredient it measures.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about adding fractions.

vocab.def: A fraction with 1 as its numerator, showing one equal part of a whole.
vocab.sentence: A unit fraction like 1/8 is one piece of the cup.

vocab.def: The same denominator in two fractions, so their pieces are the same size.
vocab.sentence: Fractions with like denominators are easy to add.

vocab.def: A fraction whose numerator is greater than or equal to its denominator.
vocab.sentence: The improper fraction 10/8 is greater than 1.
vocab.morphology: im- means not; proper means expected or regular

vocab.def: A number made of a whole number and a fraction.
vocab.nonExample: 10/8, which has no whole number part
vocab.sentence: The mixed number 1 2/8 means 1 whole and 2 eighths.

vocab.def: To break a number into smaller parts that add up to it.
vocab.sentence: Sana can decompose 10/8 as 8/8 plus 2/8.
vocab.everyday: To rot or break down slowly, like leaves on the ground

misconceptions.belief: When you add fractions, you add the numerators and the denominators.
misconceptions.why: Students treat a fraction as two separate whole numbers instead of a count of pieces of one size.
misconceptions.fix: Say the fractions with their unit names, 3 eighths plus 4 eighths, and show that the pieces stay eighths on a strip.

errorCase.story: Kai adds 3/8 cup of raisins and 4/8 cup of pretzels.
steps: Add the tops: 3 + 4 = 7.
Add the bottoms too: 8 + 8 = 16.
errorCase.explain: The denominator names the size of the pieces, and the pieces stay eighths. 3 eighths plus 4 eighths is 7 eighths, so the sum is 7/8.

misconceptions.belief: To multiply a whole number by a fraction, multiply the whole number by the numerator and by the denominator.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the whole-number rule of multiplying every number they see.
misconceptions.fix: Write 4 × 3/8 as 4 groups of 3 eighths and count the eighths on a number line, so the pieces stay eighths.

errorCase.story: Lena finds 4 × 3/8.
steps: I multiply 4 by the numerator and by the denominator: 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 8 = 32.
errorCase.explain: 4 × 3/8 means 4 groups of 3 eighths, which is 12 eighths. The pieces stay eighths, so the answer is 12/8, or 1 4/8.

misconceptions.belief: When subtracting mixed numbers, subtract the smaller fraction from the larger one in each place.
misconceptions.why: Students avoid regrouping a whole and subtract whichever numerator is smaller from whichever is greater.
misconceptions.fix: Rename the top mixed number so its fraction part is large enough, for example 3 1/4 as 2 5/4, before subtracting.

errorCase.story: Pablo subtracts 1 3/4 from 3 1/4.
steps: Subtract the wholes: 3 − 1 = 2.
The fractions are 3/4 and 1/4, so I subtract 3/4 − 1/4 = 2/4.
The answer is 2 2/4.
errorCase.explain: The problem takes 3/4 away from 1/4, so regroup first: 3 1/4 = 2 5/4. Then 2 5/4 − 1 3/4 = 1 2/4.

misconceptions.belief: A mixed number is a mix of two different fractions.
misconceptions.why: In everyday English, to mix means to combine different things, so students expect two fractions.
misconceptions.fix: Show 1 2/8 as one whole strip plus two eighths and say 'one whole and two eighths' every time.

reading.title: Trail Mix for the Hike
reading.text: Sana is making trail mix for the hiking club. She pours 3/8 cup of raisins and 4/8 cup of pretzels into a bowl. The fractions have like denominators, so she adds the numerators and keeps the 8: the bowl holds 7/8 cup. Then she adds 3/8 cup of seeds, and the sum is 10/8 cup. That is an improper fraction. She can decompose it as 8/8 plus 2/8, so it is the mixed number 1 2/8 cups. She scoops out 5/8 cup for a taste test and subtracts to get 5/8 cup left. Later Sana fills 4 bags with 3/8 cup of nuts each. Four times 3/8 is 12/8, or 1 4/8 cups in all.
reading.simple: Sana pours 3/8 cup of raisins and 4/8 cup of pretzels into a bowl. The fractions have like denominators, so she adds the numerators and keeps the 8. The bowl holds 7/8 cup. She adds 3/8 cup of seeds, and the sum is 10/8 cup, an improper fraction. She decomposes it as 8/8 plus 2/8, so it is the mixed number 1 2/8 cups. She takes out 5/8 cup and has 5/8 cup left. She fills 4 bags with 3/8 cup of nuts each. That is 12/8, or 1 4/8 cups in all.

questions.q: How much raisin did Sana pour into the bowl?
questions.a: 3/8 cup

questions.q: Why does Sana keep the 8 when she adds 3/8 and 4/8?
questions.a: The pieces are all eighths, so only the number of eighths changes: 3 eighths plus 4 eighths is 7 eighths.

questions.q: How does decomposing 10/8 help show the mixed number?
questions.a: 10/8 = 8/8 + 2/8, and 8/8 is one whole, so the amount is 1 whole and 2 eighths.

wdntb.why: 7/8, 5/8 and 3/8 are all less than 1 whole. 10/8 is greater than 1 whole, and it is an improper fraction.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a number line cut into eighths with hops of 3/8, 4/8 and 3/8 starting at 0. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: When you add two fractions with the same denominator, the denominator of the sum stays the same.
asn.why: The pieces are still the same size, and you only count more of them.

asn.claim: The sum of two fractions that are each less than 1 is less than 1.
asn.why: 3/8 + 4/8 is 7/8, which is less than 1, but 5/8 + 4/8 is 9/8, which is greater than 1.

wyr.q: Would you rather write 12/8 cups as a mixed number or as an improper fraction when you measure?

compare.b: Sol thinks of 3/8 as 3 copies of 1/8, so 4 × 3/8 is 12 copies of 1/8, which is 12/8.
compare.prompt: Both strategies give 12/8. How are they alike, and which one shows why the denominator stays 8?

debate.claim: Mixed numbers are easier to understand than improper fractions.
debate.forEvidence: 1 4/8 cups is easy to measure: fill 1 whole cup and then 4 eighths more.
debate.againstEvidence: Improper fractions like 12/8 are easier to add and subtract, because there is only one number to work with.

listening.script: Listen to Dante mix punch for a class party. He pours 5/6 liter of apple juice into a pitcher. Then he adds 4/6 liter of orange juice. Both amounts are sixths, so he adds the numerators: 5 plus 4 is 9, and the pitcher holds 9/6 liter. His friend Elsa says it should be 9/12 because 6 plus 6 is 12. Dante shows her that the pieces are still sixths. Then he writes 9/6 as 6/6 plus 3/6, which is the mixed number 1 3/6 liters.

tasks.q: How much punch is in the pitcher?
tasks.why: 5 sixths plus 4 sixths is 9 sixths, and the pieces stay sixths.

tasks.q: Elsa says the answer is 9/12. What is her error?
options: She added the denominators, but the pieces are still sixths.
She forgot to add the numerators.
tasks.why: Adding fractions with like denominators changes the number of pieces, not the size of the pieces.

story.title: The Trail Mix Table
story.goal: make enough trail mix for every member of the hiking club
story.intro: The hiking club leaves on Saturday morning, and Sana is in charge of the trail mix. Every ingredient is measured in eighths of a cup, so she must add, subtract and multiply fractions carefully.

beats.lead: Sana combines two ingredients in the big bowl and writes down how much is in it.
beats.success: She counts the eighths and keeps the denominator, so the bowl total matches the scoops.
beats.redirect: The total looks too small for the bowl, so Sana recounts the eighths and keeps the denominator the same.

beats.lead: Kai asks how much trail mix is left after a taste test.
beats.success: Sana takes the eighths away and finds the amount left, which matches what is in the bowl.
beats.redirect: The bowl has more than her answer says, so Sana lines up her eighths on a strip and counts again.

beats.lead: The club needs several bags, each with the same scoop of nuts.
beats.success: Sana counts the repeated eighths and renames the answer as a mixed number for the measuring cup.
beats.redirect: Her total is far too small, so she thinks of the scoop as repeated unit fractions and counts again.

story.ending: Every hiker gets a bag, and Sana can explain how each amount was added, subtracted or multiplied.

panels.says: I added 3/8 cup of raisins and 4/8 cup of pretzels and got 7/16 cup.
Look at the pieces. Both amounts are eighths. Do the pieces change size when we add?
No, they are still eighths. I counted 3 eighths and 4 eighths, which is 7 eighths.
Right! So 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 cup.
I keep the denominator because the pieces stay the same size.

predict.q: Kai says 3/8 + 4/8 is 7/16. Before Sana answers, predict what the sum really is.
predict.why: 3 eighths plus 4 eighths is 7 eighths, and the pieces stay eighths.

transfer.relationship: Pieces of the same size can be counted together, and the size of the piece does not change
phrasings: 3 eighths plus 4 eighths is 7 eighths
Hops of 3/8 and 4/8 on a number line land on 7/8
3 copies of 1/8 and 4 copies of 1/8 make 7 copies of 1/8

decoys.why: The denominators were added, but the pieces are still eighths.
This subtracts the amounts, so the result would be 1/8, not 7/8.

modeling.title: Planning trail mix for the hike
modeling.scenario: A fictional hiking club is filling 4 bags with trail mix. Each bag gets 3/8 cup of raisins and 2/8 cup of seeds.
assumptions: Every bag gets exactly the same amounts.
No raisins or seeds are spilled.
The scoops are measured exactly to the line.
prompts: How much trail mix goes in one bag?
How many cups of raisins and how many cups of seeds are needed for all 4 bags?
What would change if the club filled 6 bags instead of 4?
limits: Real scoops are never exactly level, so some bags would have a little more.
We ignored the trail mix that sticks to the bowl.

sentence.because: The sum is 7/8 because 3 eighths plus 4 eighths is 7 eighths.
sentence.but: The fractions 3/8 and 4/8 are different amounts, but they have like denominators.
sentence.so: The pieces are all eighths, so the denominator stays 8.

diagnostic.prompt: Solve 5/6 + 4/6, 7/8 − 3/8 and 3 × 2/5. Write each answer as a fraction or a mixed number and tell how you know.
lookFor: Adds or subtracts the numerators and keeps the denominator
Writes 3 × 2/5 as 6 fifths and renames it 1 1/5
Explains the answers with unit fractions, a strip or a number line
diagnostic.language: Let the student show each answer with fraction strips before explaining. If the strips are right, the barrier is the words numerator, denominator and mixed number.

extension.task: Write a story problem that needs 5 × 3/4, solve it, and show the answer as a mixed number.
extension.reasoning: Explain why 5 × 3/4 is greater than 3 but less than 4.

en.learning: Your child is learning to add and subtract fractions with the same bottom number and to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
en.say: When the pieces are the same size, we count the pieces and the size does not change.
en.ask: A recipe needs 3/4 cup of milk for one batch. How much milk do we need for 3 batches?
en.activity: Use measuring cups to pour 1/4 cup scoops of rice into a bowl. Find how many scoops make 1 cup, then 1 1/2 cups, and say each amount as a fraction.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a sumar y restar fracciones con el mismo denominador y a multiplicar una fracción por un número entero.
es.say: Cuando las partes tienen el mismo tamaño, contamos las partes y el tamaño no cambia.
es.ask: Una receta necesita 3/4 de taza de leche para una tanda. ¿Cuánta leche necesitamos para 3 tandas?
es.activity: Usen tazas medidoras para echar cucharadas de 1/4 de taza de arroz en un tazón. Averigüen cuántas cucharadas llenan 1 taza, y luego 1 1/2 tazas, y digan cada cantidad como fracción.

skills.objective: Students connect fractions with denominators 10 and 100 to decimal notation, add tenths and hundredths, and compare decimals to hundredths by reasoning about place value.
skills.studentObjective: I can write tenths and hundredths as fractions and as decimals, and I can tell which decimal is greater.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why one decimal is greater than another using because, but and so with the words tenth, hundredth and equivalent decimals.
successCriteria: I write a fraction with denominator 10 or 100 as a decimal, and the other way around.
I rename tenths as hundredths so I can add or compare.
I compare two decimals and write the comparison with greater than or less than.
I explain my comparison using place value words.
skills.bigIdea: The place right of the decimal point names tenths and the next place names hundredths, so decimals are compared by matching place values, not by counting digits.

syntax: ___ tenths is the same as ___ hundredths.
___ is greater than ___ because ___ hundredths is greater than ___ hundredths.
discourse: Justify a comparison using place value
Explain a rename step before adding

domains.listening: Students listen to a ribbon story and decide which ribbon is longer and why.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they read a decimal aloud using tenths and hundredths.
domains.reading: Students read a rain report and underline each decimal and the fraction it matches.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares two decimals.

vocab.def: One of 10 equal parts of a whole, written 1/10 or 0.1.
vocab.sentence: One tenth of an inch is 0.1 inch.
vocab.morphology: tenth is ten plus th, the ending for a part of a set

vocab.def: One of 100 equal parts of a whole, written 1/100 or 0.01.
vocab.sentence: A hundredth is smaller than a tenth.

vocab.def: The dot in a decimal that separates whole numbers from parts of a whole.
vocab.example: In 0.25, the decimal point comes after the 0
vocab.nonExample: A period at the end of a sentence
vocab.sentence: Ben lines up the decimal points before he compares.
vocab.everyday: A sharp end, like the tip of a pencil, or one score in a game

vocab.def: Decimals that name the same amount, even if they are written with different digits.
vocab.sentence: The decimals 0.3 and 0.30 are equivalent decimals.
vocab.morphology: equi- means equal; valent means worth

vocab.def: To decide whether one number is greater than, less than or equal to another.
vocab.example: To compare 0.3 and 0.25, write both in hundredths
vocab.sentence: Ben and Imani compare the rain on two days.

misconceptions.belief: A decimal with more digits is always greater.
misconceptions.why: With whole numbers, more digits really does mean a greater number, and students carry that rule over to the digits after the decimal point.
misconceptions.fix: Rename both decimals with the same number of places, like 0.30 and 0.25, and compare the hundredths on a grid.

errorCase.story: Imani compares 0.3 inch and 0.25 inch of rain.
steps: 0.25 has 25 after the decimal point and 0.3 has 3.
25 is greater than 3, so 0.25 is greater than 0.3.
Tuesday had more rain than Monday.
errorCase.explain: Match the places first. 0.3 is 0.30, and 30 hundredths is greater than 25 hundredths, so Monday had more rain.

misconceptions.belief: To add 3/10 and 4/100, add the numerators and add the denominators.
misconceptions.why: Students treat each fraction as two separate numbers and skip the step of making equal-sized pieces.
misconceptions.fix: Rename 3/10 as 30/100 on a hundred grid, then count hundredths together.

errorCase.story: Ben adds 3/10 inch and 4/100 inch of rain.
steps: The denominators are 10 and 100, which are different.
I add the tops and the bottoms: 3 + 4 = 7 and 10 + 100 = 110.
errorCase.explain: The pieces are different sizes, so rename 3/10 as 30/100 first. Then 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100, which is 0.34.

misconceptions.belief: The fraction 4/100 is written as 0.4.
misconceptions.why: Students write the digit right after the decimal point without checking which place it belongs in.
misconceptions.fix: Use a place value chart with tenths and hundredths columns so the 4 goes in the hundredths column and a 0 holds the tenths place.

errorCase.story: Ben writes 4/100 as a decimal.
steps: The fraction 4/100 means 4 hundredths.
I write the 4 right after the decimal point: 0.4.
errorCase.explain: The first place after the decimal point is the tenths place. For 4 hundredths, write a 0 in the tenths place: 0.04.

misconceptions.belief: Tenths means the same as tens.
misconceptions.why: The words tens and tenths sound almost the same, so students hear them as one idea.
misconceptions.fix: Say the th aloud and link each word to a picture: tens are big groups of 10 ones, tenths are small pieces, 1 of 10 equal parts.

reading.title: The Rain Report
reading.text: In science class, Imani measures rain with a gauge. On Monday it rained 0.3 inch, which is 3/10 of an inch. On Tuesday it rained 0.25 inch, which is 25/100 of an inch. Imani thinks 0.25 is greater because 25 is greater than 3. Her partner Ben says to compare the tenths and the hundredths carefully. He lines up the decimal points and writes 0.3 as 0.30, so 0.3 and 0.30 are equivalent decimals. Now it is clear that 30 hundredths is greater than 25 hundredths, so Monday had more rain. On Wednesday it rained 4/100 inch. To add Monday and Wednesday, Ben renames 3/10 as 30/100. Then 30/100 plus 4/100 is 34/100, or 0.34 inch.
reading.simple: In science class, Imani measures rain. On Monday it rained 0.3 inch, which is 3/10 of an inch. On Tuesday it rained 0.25 inch, which is 25/100 of an inch. Imani thinks 0.25 is greater because 25 is greater than 3. Ben lines up the decimal points and writes 0.3 as 0.30, so they are equivalent decimals. Now they compare: 30 hundredths is greater than 25 hundredths. Monday had more rain. On Wednesday it rained 4/100 inch. Ben renames 3/10 as 30/100. Then 30/100 plus 4/100 is 34/100, or 0.34 inch.

questions.q: How much did it rain on Tuesday?
questions.a: 0.25 inch, which is 25/100 of an inch

questions.q: Why does Ben write 0.3 as 0.30 before he compares?
questions.a: Then both decimals are in hundredths, so he can compare 30 hundredths with 25 hundredths.

questions.q: How much rain fell on Monday and Wednesday together?

wdntb.why: 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 all name 3 tenths. 0.03 names 3 hundredths, which is a much smaller amount.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two hundred-square grids: one with 3 full columns shaded and one with 2 full columns and 5 more squares shaded. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Writing a zero at the end of a decimal, like 0.3 to 0.30, does not change its value.
asn.why: 3 tenths and 30 hundredths name the same amount of the whole.

asn.claim: A decimal with more digits after the decimal point is greater.
asn.why: 0.31 is greater than 0.3, but 0.25 is less than 0.3. You have to compare the place values.

wyr.q: Would you rather show 0.34 on a hundred-square grid or with 3 dimes and 4 pennies?

compare.a: Ana compares 0.3 and 0.25 by writing both in hundredths: 30/100 and 25/100.
compare.b: Luis compares them on a number line from 0 to 1 cut into tenths and sees that 0.25 is between 0.2 and 0.3.
compare.prompt: Both strategies tell which is greater. How does each one show that 0.3 is greater than 0.25?

debate.claim: A decimal with more digits is a greater number, just like with whole numbers.
debate.forEvidence: With whole numbers, more digits means a greater number, like 125 and 36, so it seems the same rule should work.
debate.againstEvidence: Decimals follow place value, so 0.3 is greater than 0.25 even though 0.25 has more digits.

listening.script: Listen to Teo measure ribbon for a craft project. His blue ribbon is 0.7 meter long, and his red ribbon is 0.65 meter long. At first he thinks the red ribbon is longer, because 65 is greater than 7. Then he writes 0.7 as 0.70, so both numbers are in hundredths. Now he compares 70 hundredths with 65 hundredths. Seventy is greater, so the blue ribbon is longer. The blue ribbon is 5 hundredths of a meter longer than the red one.

tasks.q: Which ribbon is longer?
tasks.why: 0.7 is 0.70, and 70 hundredths is greater than 65 hundredths.

tasks.q: At first Teo thought the red ribbon was longer. What was his error?
options: He compared 65 and 7 without matching the place values.
He forgot to add the two lengths.
He thought a hundredth is greater than a tenth.
tasks.why: The 65 is in hundredths and the 7 is in tenths, so the numbers cannot be compared until the places match.

story.title: The Rain Gauge Report
story.goal: report which day had the most rain and how much fell in all
story.intro: Imani's science class keeps a rain gauge in the school garden. At the end of the week, the principal wants a report that ranks the rainy days and adds up the rainfall.

beats.lead: Imani reads the gauge for two days and decides which day had more rain.
beats.success: She matches the places and compares hundredths, so her ranking agrees with the gauge.
beats.redirect: Her ranking looks odd next to the gauge, so Imani writes both decimals in hundredths and compares again.

beats.lead: Ben reads a very small amount of rain from Wednesday and writes it as a decimal.
beats.success: He puts a zero in the tenths place, and the decimal matches the fraction on the gauge.
beats.redirect: His decimal looks too big, so Ben checks which place each digit belongs in.

beats.lead: The principal asks how much rain fell on two of the days together.
beats.success: Imani renames tenths as hundredths and adds, and the principal writes the total in the report.
beats.redirect: Imani realizes the pieces were different sizes, so she renames one amount and adds again.

story.ending: The garden report is posted on the board, and Imani can tell visitors how she compared every day.

panels.says: Tuesday had 0.25 inch of rain and Monday had 0.3 inch, so Tuesday had more.
Why do you say Tuesday had more?
Because 25 is greater than 3.
Let us write 0.3 as 0.30. Now we compare 30 hundredths and 25 hundredths.
Oh! Thirty is greater than twenty-five, so Monday had more rain.

predict.q: Imani says 0.25 inch is more rain than 0.3 inch. Before Ben answers, predict which day really had more rain.
predict.why: 0.3 is 0.30, and 30 hundredths is greater than 25 hundredths.

transfer.relationship: Fractions with denominator 10 or 100 and decimals name the same amounts, and place values must match before comparing
phrasings: 3 of the 10 equal parts of an inch
30 hundredths, written 0.30
On a number line from 0 to 1, 0.3 is at the third tenth mark

decoys.why: 3/100 is 0.03, which is 3 hundredths, a much smaller amount.

decoys.text: 0.3 is less than 0.25 because 3 is less than 25
decoys.why: This compares the digits without matching the place values.

modeling.title: Planning the rain report
modeling.scenario: A fictional garden club records rain with a gauge each day. The garden needs 0.6 inch of rain this week, and three days have already been measured.
assumptions: The gauge is read exactly to the hundredth.
Each day's rain is measured once and not counted twice.
